title: Pascal, Fermat, and the Birth of Probability Theory (1654)
explainer: Modern probability theory is usually dated to 1654, when the gambler Chevalier de Méré brought Blaise Pascal a puzzle about fairly dividing stakes in an interrupted dice game. The letters Pascal exchanged with Pierre de Fermat working through that problem are the episode historians point to as the start of probability as a mathematical subject, decades before anyone wrote down a formal definition of probability itself.

title: Thomas Bayes's Posthumous Essay (1763)
explainer: Bayes' theorem is named for a result that its author, the English minister Thomas Bayes, never published himself. He left the essay among his papers when he died, and it was his friend Richard Price who edited it and had it presented to the Royal Society in 1763. It took further work by Pierre-Simon Laplace decades later before the idea became the widely used tool it is today.
